wa_south_face_4.blurb: The south side of Beacon Rock, a lone basalt monolith rising from the Washington bank of the Columbia Gorge. This is mostly a traditional wall: steep, sustained lines up solid columnar rock, which is unusual in a gorge where much of the stone is crumbly. Most of the climbing sits between 5.10 and 5.12, with a smaller number of moderates from 5.6 to 5.9 and a few bolted lines and one aid route. Pitches are long and the face is exposed to the wind, which can make communication with a partner hard and chilly on a blustery day. Bring a full trad rack and a helmet, and expect the popular moderates to see weekend traffic.
wa_south_face_4.parking_note: Use the main Beacon Rock lot and leave the car at its east end, close to the climbers' information board.
wa_south_face_4.approach: The climbers' trail begins just left of the information board and drops around the east side of the rock to the south face. The paved summit stairway on the other side is not the way in.

wa_calendar_butte.blurb: A steep, roughly 160-foot wall beside the Walker Valley off-road area, north of Arlington. Nearly all of it is bolted sport climbing on vertical to overhanging terrain, with a handful of well-protected trad lines and a couple of boulder problems. Most routes fall in the 5.10 to 5.12 range, with only a few easier lines. The main wall faces south and dries quickly after rain, so it is a popular choice for cold sunny days, while the shadier sections such as Shadow Wall and Creek Wall suit hot ones. The sunniest part gets very warm by mid morning in summer. Bring a rope of at least 70 meters.
wa_calendar_butte.parking_note: Park next to the concrete blocks at the end of the drivable road if there is room. If it is full, a narrow pullout lies about 100 yards east beside Pilchuck Creek; keep clear of other cars.
wa_calendar_butte.approach: Roughly two miles on gravel forest roads with a few small creek crossings that logs and rocks make easy. Waterproof shoes are handy.

wa_sehome_arboretum.blurb: A wooded city park on a hill beside the Western Washington University campus in Bellingham, with scattered sandstone boulders and short cliff bands. It is mostly a bouldering spot, with problems from VB through V4 making up most of what is here and a few harder ones, plus short top-rope lines, a few trad leads and a handful of bolted routes. Climbs are brief, and some landings are poor, so pads and a spotter matter. The sandstone is soft and fragile when wet, so wait until it is fully dry; in winter that can take more than a week. Expect hikers, runners and students on the trails around the rocks.
wa_sehome_arboretum.parking_note: The park entrance is on Bill McDonald Parkway at 25th Street. Leave the car outside the yellow gate at the foot of the hill, or drive up toward the summit if the road is open.

wa_c_king_pins.blurb: A section of the south-facing Sunshine Wall in Echo Basin, the small coulee just south of Frenchman Coulee near Vantage. The King Pins hold some of the tallest columns of basalt in the area and are regarded as some of its best rock. Climbing is mostly trad, with a good share of sport, from the 5.7 range up into 5.11, though the bulk of routes sit between 5.8 and 5.11. Cracks and bolted aretes are the main themes. The wall is busy, with climbers on it most weekends, so arriving early helps. It gets hot in warm weather; early mornings and evenings are shadier, and cool sunny days suit it well. Watch for loose flakes.
wa_c_king_pins.parking_note: Use the main climbers' lot off Vantage Road, then walk in from there.
wa_c_king_pins.approach: Hike south past the Agathla Tower formation and up onto the mesa, then take the left fork and descend the first gully between the pillars to reach the base of the wall.

wa_lower_band.blurb: The lower of two basalt cliff bands above the Columbia River at Wallula Gap, a short way off the highway. The rock here is sturdier than the upper band, though still fractured in places, and a helmet is a sensible choice. Routes are short, mostly 20 to 35 feet, and trad and sport are split fairly evenly, often sharing anchors. Most climbs fall between 5.7 and 5.10, so it suits newer leaders as well as those looking for quick laps. Wind can be strong enough to make talking with a belayer difficult, and rattlesnakes live in the gap. Summer mornings and winter afternoons tend to be the most comfortable times to go.
wa_lower_band.parking_note: Pull off into the roadside parking area along the highway through the gap; the larger, second pullout farther south is the one to use.
wa_lower_band.approach: A short trail begins across the highway from the north end of the pullout, marked by a small sign. It climbs steeply at the start and finish and reaches the base of the cliff in a few minutes.

wv_rhododendron_trail_boulders.blurb: A cluster of boulders strung along the Rhododendron Trail in Coopers Rock State Forest, near Morgantown. It is all bouldering, with problems from the easiest grades up through V8; the middle grades around V3 and V4 are the most common. The coarse sandstone has a gritty feel, with sloping holds, rounded edges and shallow pockets, and grades have a reputation for being stiff. Rhodo Cave stays dry during rain, though it can sweat on hot humid days, while the open boulders need roughly a day to dry after a hard storm. Don't climb wet rock, brush off chalk and tick marks, and pack out all trash. The forest as a whole is busy with hikers and bikers.
wv_rhododendron_trail_boulders.parking_note: Drive in off Exit 15 of I-68 and leave the car at the trailhead, then walk the Rhododendron Trail to the sub-areas.
